title: Colombian Marine Fossils Hint at Evolutionary Leap Without Mass Extinction Breakthrough
body:
A fossil assemblage unearthed in the Andes of central Colombia is reshaping scientists’ understanding of how marine life navigated the Jurassic‑Cretaceous transition, suggesting that some groups may have persisted and evolved without the dramatic die‑offs traditionally associated with that interval. The discovery, made in a limestone quarry near the town of Villa de Leyva, contains an unprecedented mixture of ancient Jurassic survivors alongside emerging Cretaceous species, offering a rare glimpse into a possible evolutionary bridge that operated without a wholesale extinction event.

The research team, a collaboration between paleontologists from McGill University and Colombia’s Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas, examined more than 200 fossil specimens recovered from the so‑called “La Quinta” formation. Among the finds are well‑preserved ammonites, bivalves, and marine reptiles that belong to lineages thought to have vanished by the end of the Jurassic. In the same layers, however, they also identified early representatives of groups that would later dominate the Cretaceous seas, such as the highly diversified mosasaurids and certain planktonic foraminifera. Radiometric dating places the strata at roughly 145 million years old, right at the Jurassic‑Cretaceous boundary, a period that has long been considered a “quiet” interval in Earth’s mass‑extinction history.

What makes the Colombian site extraordinary is the degree of ecological overlap it records. In most fossil records, Jurassic and Cretaceous assemblages appear in distinct, non‑overlapping horizons, reinforcing the notion of a clean turnover. Here, the co‑occurrence of taxa suggests that at least some marine organisms managed to survive the subtle environmental shifts of the late Jurassic and gradually gave rise to newer forms. The researchers propose that regional factors—such as the relative stability of the proto‑Caribbean seaway, localized nutrient influxes, and a lack of large‑scale volcanic activity—could have created refugia where species persisted long enough to evolve in situ.

The findings challenge the prevailing view that the Jurassic‑Cretaceous boundary, though less dramatic than the end‑Cretaceous event, still involved a series of moderate extinction pulses that cleared ecological space for new groups. Instead, the Colombian record points to a more nuanced scenario where evolutionary turnover was, at least in some marine provinces, a gradual process driven by ecological opportunity rather than catastrophic loss. This perspective aligns with recent studies of other “transitional” deposits in Europe and Asia that have hinted at lingering Jurassic lineages, but the Colombian site provides the most comprehensive and well‑dated example to date.

Beyond its implications for deep‑time biodiversity dynamics, the discovery also underscores the importance of South America’s fossil record, which has historically been under‑represented in global paleobiological syntheses. The Andes’ complex tectonic history has preserved a mosaic of sedimentary environments, yet political and logistical hurdles have limited systematic exploration. The success of this joint venture highlights how international collaborations can unlock hidden chapters of Earth’s history, encouraging further fieldwork in similarly understudied regions.

Looking ahead, the team plans to expand their investigation to adjacent formations and employ high‑resolution isotopic analyses to reconstruct paleo‑temperature and ocean chemistry at the boundary. Such data could clarify whether subtle climate shifts, rather than abrupt catastrophes, drove the observed evolutionary patterns. If the Colombian model proves applicable elsewhere, it may prompt a revision of how paleontologists conceptualize mass‑extinction dynamics, emphasizing the role of regional refugia and incremental adaptation. As more discoveries emerge, the story of life’s resilience across deep time continues to unfold, offering fresh insights into the mechanisms that have shaped the planet’s ever‑changing biosphere.
